title: Unit – 2 : Session – 2 : SLO – 1 | Operational concepts
sections: Section A – Match the Following (Answers)
1. MAR → C. Holds addresses for memory access
2. MDR → D. Temporary storage of data
3. IR → A. Holds the instruction currently being executed
4. PC → B. Points to the next instruction
5. General-purpose Registers → E. Scratch-pad registers for holding data and intermediate results
Section B – Fill in the Blanks
The PROCESSOR (CPU) executes tasks by following a sequence of instructions.
The MAR register holds the address of the memory location to be accessed.
The instruction LOAD loads data from a memory location into a register.
The MDR register stores data being transferred between memory and processor.
STORE instructions overwrite the content of the destination register or memory location.
Section C – Activity Task

Instruction: Load R2, LOC | Operation: reads the contents of memory location LOC and copies them into register R2 | Involved: PC, MAR, MDR, memory location LOC, register R2 | Outcome: R2 ← [LOC]; memory content unchanged (read is non-destructive).

Instruction: Add LOCA, R0 | Operation: adds the contents of memory location LOCA to register R0 | Involved: MAR, MDR, memory location LOCA, register R0, ALU | Outcome: R0 ← R0 + [LOCA]; LOCA unchanged, R0 overwritten with the sum.
Section D – True or False
The Program Counter (PC) holds the data that is currently being executed. — FALSE (it holds the address of the next instruction)
The Memory Address Register (MAR) holds the instruction being fetched from memory. — FALSE (it holds the address; MDR holds the instruction/data)
The contents of R2 and R3 are altered during the execution of Add R4, R2, R3. — FALSE (only R4 changes)
Load instructions preserve the original contents of the memory location. — TRUE
General-purpose registers can be used to store intermediate results of operations. — TRUE
